title: Hand Signals, Acoustic Signals & Markings
whatItIs: Not every safety sign is a board. Hand signals guide crane and vehicle moves, alarms and lights warn of danger, and stripes and lines mark hazards and routes.

keyFacts.text: The signaller MUST be able to see all the manoeuvres without being put in danger.
The signaller's duties MUST be only directing the manoeuvre and keeping nearby workers safe.
An operator who can't carry on safely MUST stop and ask the signaller for new instructions.
The acoustic signal for evacuation MUST be continuous.

keyFacts: Obstacles and drops: yellow/black or red/white stripes at about 45°. Vehicle routes: lines, preferably white or yellow.

visual.caption: Standard hand signals (Safety Signs and Signals Regulations)

rows: Both arms out horizontally, palms forward
Right arm pointing up, palm forward
Both hands clasped at chest height
Right arm up, palm forward, slowly circling
Right arm down, palm in, slowly circling
Both arms pointing up, palms forward
notes: Signals from the crane and agricultural codes named in Schedule 2 (eg BS 7121) may be used instead.

onTheTest.question: A signaller raises both arms above their head with the palms facing forwards. What does this mean?
onTheTest.why: In the standard code, DANGER (emergency stop) is both arms pointing upwards, palms forward. STOP uses the right arm only.

onTheTest.question: How must an acoustic signal for evacuation sound?
onTheTest.why: Safety Signs and Signals Regulations, Schedule 1 Part VII: the signal for evacuation must be continuous.

traps: Take signals from one signaller only, unless special arrangements have been made.
A flashing light means greater danger or more urgency than a steady one.
The signaller should be easy to spot: a distinctive bright jacket, helmet, armbands or bats.
